title: Reading Clues in Shared Sequences
endLine: Shared sequences point to relatives and candidate functions; experiments confirm them.

scenes.tts: How can a string of letters reveal what an unknown protein does? Children with smooth brains led researchers to a human gene called L I S one. Its sequence alone did not say what the protein does.
scenes.caption: How can a string of letters reveal what an unknown protein does? Children with smooth brains led researchers to a human gene called LIS1. Its sequence alone did not say what the protein does.
scenes.visual: Carried alignment workbench filling over 60% of frame height, no molecular structures. A glowing schematic strip of amino-acid letter blocks labeled 'Human LIS1' slides into the upper lane and settles before the narrator names it, with a pulsing '?' beside it. The lower lane stays empty, waiting for a relative.
scenes.narration: How can a string of letters reveal what an unknown protein does? Children with smooth brains led researchers to a human gene called LIS1. Its sequence alone did not say what the protein does.

scenes.visual: The 'Human LIS1' strip dims gently in place while the title 'Reading Clues in Shared Sequences' fades in at center in high-contrast text for 2 seconds, then clears back to the workbench.

scenes.tts: Sequence alignment slides two letter strips past each other until matching positions line up. The clue came from a mould gene, nud F. In 1995, its protein matched human L I S one at forty-two percent of aligned positions. Chance rarely matches that much along a whole protein. So it pointed to homology: inheritance from one shared ancestor.
scenes.caption: Sequence alignment slides two letter strips past each other until matching positions line up. The clue came from a mould gene, nudF. In 1995, its protein matched human LIS1 at 42 percent of aligned positions. Chance rarely matches that much along a whole protein. So it pointed to homology: inheritance from one shared ancestor.
scenes.visual: Same workbench. 'Human LIS1' returns to full brightness in the upper lane; a second schematic strip labeled 'Mould nudF' enters below and slides horizontally until matching tiles snap into glowing vertical columns as alignment is described. A schematic match bar fills to '42% match', and a bracket joins both strips above the label 'Homology'.
scenes.narration: Sequence alignment slides two letter strips past each other until matching positions line up. The clue came from a mould gene, nudF. In 1995, its protein matched human LIS1 at 42 percent of aligned positions. Chance rarely matches that much along a whole protein. So it pointed to homology: inheritance from one shared ancestor.

scenes.tts: A match lets knowledge from one organism become a clue in another. Nud stands for nuclear distribution: mould mutants leave their nuclei bunched. Other nud genes encode parts of cytoplasmic dynein, a motor that moves nuclei along protein tracks called microtubules. Mammalian cell experiments confirmed that L I S one binds dynein.
scenes.caption: A match lets knowledge from one organism become a clue in another. Nud stands for nuclear distribution: mould mutants leave their nuclei bunched. Other nud genes encode parts of cytoplasmic dynein, a motor that moves nuclei along protein tracks called microtubules. Mammalian cell experiments confirmed that LIS1 binds dynein.
scenes.visual: Same workbench. Beside the aligned 'Human LIS1' and 'Mould nudF' strips, a schematic mould filament shows its nuclei bunched at one end, labeled 'nud mutant'. Below, a schematic microtubule rail appears with a schematic dynein motor moving a nucleus along it; a dashed clue arrow bridges from 'Mould nudF' to 'Human LIS1', turning solid with a subtle check mark when mammalian cell experiments confirm binding.
scenes.narration: A match lets knowledge from one organism become a clue in another. Nud stands for nuclear distribution: mould mutants leave their nuclei bunched. Other nud genes encode parts of cytoplasmic dynein, a motor that moves nuclei along protein tracks called microtubules. Mammalian cell experiments confirmed that LIS1 binds dynein.

scenes.tts: Suppose two species share the exact same sequence feature. Does that guarantee they are closest relatives, or could another history explain it?
scenes.caption: Suppose two species share the exact same sequence feature. Does that guarantee they are closest relatives, or could another history explain it?
scenes.visual: Same workbench. The aligned strips morph into two generic schematic tracks labeled 'Species one' and 'Species two' sharing one glowing aligned block. Below them, a simple schematic branching tree fades in with a pulsing '?' over its branches, and the question card 'Closest relatives, or another cause?' settles above the tree.
scenes.narration: Suppose two species share the exact same sequence feature. Does that guarantee they are closest relatives, or could another history explain it?

scenes.visual: Thinking pause (4.5 seconds). The question 'Closest relatives, or another cause?' stays clearly on screen while the shared block on both schematic tracks and the '?' on the schematic tree breathe with a slow ambient pulse.

scenes.tts: A match alone cannot guarantee closest relatives. Two lineages can gain the same feature separately, a trap called convergence. Or both can keep an ancestral state, present before they split. Only a shared derived change, gained once on one shared branch, shows which relatives are closest.
scenes.caption: A match alone cannot guarantee closest relatives. Two lineages can gain the same feature separately, a trap called convergence. Or both can keep an ancestral state, present before they split. Only a shared derived change, gained once on one shared branch, shows which relatives are closest.
scenes.visual: Same workbench; question card clears. On the schematic tree below the tracks, two separate glowing bursts appear on distant branches as 'Convergence' is named. Next, a glow begins at the deep root and flows to all tips as 'Ancestral state' is named. Finally, a single gain lights up on one shared inner branch leading to two sister tips, labeled 'Shared derived'.
scenes.narration: A match alone cannot guarantee closest relatives. Two lineages can gain the same feature separately, a trap called convergence. Or both can keep an ancestral state, present before they split. Only a shared derived change, gained once on one shared branch, shows which relatives are closest.

scenes.tts: An outside relative, called an outgroup, suggests which state is ancestral. Its own lineage can change too, so studies compare several outgroups. One gene's tree can also differ from the species tree. Tools like Scansite predict where a phosphate group might attach. A predicted site stays a guess until experiments find the phosphate.
scenes.caption: An outside relative, called an outgroup, suggests which state is ancestral. Its own lineage can change too, so studies compare several outgroups. scenes.visual: Same workbench. Multiple outgroup branches grow at the base of the schematic tree ('Several outgroups'), then a faint dashed species tree shifts slightly out of register behind the gene tree ('Gene tree vs species tree'). The tree recedes as a schematic sequence strip highlights a 'Scansite' candidate slot with '?', turning solid only when a schematic phosphate marker lands on it.

scenes.tts: In 1986, Robert Lefkowitz's laboratory at Duke and a Merck group cloned a beta-adrenergic receptor, which senses adrenaline. Its sequence resembled rhodopsin, the eye's light-catching pigment, seven water-avoiding membrane spans included. Every seven-span protein then known used light, so some guessed the plan meant light sensing. Instead, it marked receptors signaling through G proteins, relay proteins inside cells.

The label 'Light-sensitive only?' crosses out and transforms into 'G-protein receptors (1986)'.

scenes.tts: In 1989, Michael Reth published a letter with no experiment. He lined up published tail sequences of partner chains from immune receptors. Chains from T cells, the B cell receptor and the mast cell receptor all shared one pattern.
scenes.caption: In 1989, Michael Reth published a letter with no experiment. He lined up published tail sequences of partner chains from immune receptors. Chains from T cells, the B-cell receptor and the mast-cell receptor all shared one pattern.
scenes.visual: Same workbench. Schematic tail strips labeled 'T cell', 'B-cell receptor' and 'Mast-cell receptor' partner chains stack into alignment and illuminate one shared vertical pattern column, with the tag 'Reth, 1989: no new experiment'.
scenes.narration: In 1989, Michael Reth published a letter with no experiment. He lined up published tail sequences of partner chains from immune receptors. Chains from T cells, the B-cell receptor and the mast-cell receptor all shared one pattern.

scenes.tts: In 2007, Amit, Wides and Yarden compared the human genome with four invertebrate animals. Genomes differ in total gene number, so they adjusted for it. Per gene, humans had about two point five times as many E G F receptors. Total protein kinases were only about one point two times higher.
scenes.caption: In 2007, Amit, Wides and Yarden compared the human genome with four invertebrate animals. Genomes differ in total gene number, so they adjusted for it. Per gene, humans had about 2.5 times as many EGF receptors. Total protein kinases were only about 1.2 times higher.
scenes.visual: Same workbench. The strips transform into a genome comparison bar chart ('Human vs four invertebrates, adjusted for gene number', 2007). A dashed baseline at 1x marks the invertebrates. The 'EGF receptors' bar rises to 2.5x; the 'All protein kinases' bar rises only to 1.2x. Bar heights are drawn to these values.
